assertions.text: Output contains a @TableTest annotation
assertions.evidence: Found @TableTest annotation

assertions.text: Each policy threshold (650 for non-seniors, 600 for seniors) is verifiable from the table, in one of two ways: (a) a dedicated policy column (e.g. 'Credit threshold') beside the applicant's score, or (b) boundary rows that bracket it — within one age band, a row that qualifies just above the threshold and a row that fails at/below it, carrying different decisions.
assertions.evidence: First table has boundary rows at 64/650 (REJECTED) and 64/651 (APPROVED), and 65/600 (REJECTED) and 65/601 (APPROVED). However, third table row 'Rejected: below standard threshold, regardless of income' uses score 600 at age 40, which is below the 650 threshold but lacks a bracketing pair at age 40 showing 650 vs 651.

assertions.text: Cell values use concrete domain terms (e.g. '70', '650', 'APPROVED') — not abstract codes like 'CATEGORY_A' or '1'. Boolean true/false is acceptable for yes/no flags when the parameter type is boolean.
assertions.evidence: All values are concrete: ages (64, 65, 90, 40, 70), credit scores (650, 651, 601, 700, 620, 550, 600), results (REJECTED, APPROVED, PENDING_REVIEW), and booleans (true, false, null).

assertions.text: Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
assertions.evidence: First column(s): "Scenario", "Scenario", "Scenario"

assertions.text: Scenario names describe conditions ('Senior at lower threshold', 'Missing income') — not outcomes ('Approved', 'Rejected').
assertions.evidence: Third table contains scenario names like 'Approved: standard threshold, stable income', 'Rejected: standard threshold, no stable income', and 'Rejected: below standard threshold, regardless of income' — all begin with outcome words (Approved, Rejected).

assertions.text: Column names use domain/business language (e.g. 'Age', 'Credit score', 'Stable income', 'Decision?') — not code identifiers like 'customerAge', 'boolean'.
assertions.evidence: Columns are named 'Age', 'Credit Score', 'Has Stable Income', 'Result?' — all business language, not code identifiers.

assertions.text: At least one output column name ends with '?' (e.g. 'Decision?' or 'Status?')
assertions.evidence: Question-mark columns: Result?, Result?, Result?

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
assertions.evidence: 3 method(s) checked — no if/switch/ternary

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
assertions.evidence: Annotations in correct order: @DisplayName, @Description, @TableTest

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case.
assertions.evidence: 3 @TableTest method name(s) read as descriptive titles (no @DisplayName needed)

assertions.text: If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
assertions.evidence: @Description uses text block or is short single-line

assertions.text: The distinct concerns (age→threshold, credit boundary, income status) are each covered, without a monolithic table that re-proves unrelated rules through redundant permutations.
assertions.evidence: Third table row 'Rejected: below standard threshold, regardless of income' uses value set {true, false} to re-prove the below-threshold rejection rule twice (once per income value), creating redundant permutations of the same concern.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns.
assertions.evidence: Third table row 'Rejected: below standard threshold, regardless of income | 40 | 600 | {true, false} | REJECTED' generates two rows from one scenario, re-proving the same rule (below-threshold rejection) twice.

assertions.text: Age boundary policy, credit score categorisation, and income status are each covered by minimal scenarios.
assertions.evidence: First table covers age/credit boundaries (rows at 64/650, 64/651, 65/600, 65/601). Second table covers null income. Third table covers income status variations (true, false, null) and combines all three concerns.

assertions.text: Scenario names and @Description text do not restate values the table already shows.
assertions.evidence: First @Description states 'Standard threshold is 650; applicants aged 65+ get a lower threshold of 600' — these policy values (650, 600, 65) are already shown in the table rows and should not be restated in prose.

assertions.text: The effect of stable income on the outcome is visible from table rows, not merely implied. Two rows must differ in the stable-income column while holding credit score and age columns equal, carrying different expected decisions.
assertions.evidence: Third table rows 'Approved: standard threshold, stable income | 40 | 700 | true | APPROVED' and 'Rejected: standard threshold, no stable income | 40 | 700 | false | REJECTED' hold age and score equal (40, 700) and differ only in income (true vs false), with different decisions.

assertions.text: The build file (build.gradle) includes org.tabletest:tabletest-junit as a test dependency
assertions.evidence: Build file contains tabletest-junit

assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. A table fails if: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row.
assertions.evidence: All three tables have varying expectation values (REJECTED, APPROVED, PENDING_REVIEW) that differ from input columns and would not be satisfied by a fixed-return implementation.

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body.
assertions.evidence: Second table states 'When hasStableIncome is null, the applicant is sent to pending review regardless of age or score' — a rule not visible in the table itself. The table shows only null income → PENDING_REVIEW; the 'regardless of age or score' generalization requires the @Description.

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on.
assertions.evidence: Second method title: 'missingIncomeInformationYieldsPendingReview' — striking 'evaluator' leaves 'missing income information yields pending review', which is a domain rule (a policy decision), not a description of what the code does. The code implements the rule; the title restates the rule itself.
